explain.say: Now look at everyone joins. As more people join, others join because so many already have. See how steeply the line shoots up? That is the bandwagon effect: we join in mainly because something is popular, not because we checked it ourselves. Have you jumped on a bandwagon?

explain.say: See fear of missing out? Nobody wants to be the only one left out. That worried feeling pushes even more people to join. It works for toys, songs, fashions and even ideas and votes. What makes you feel like you might miss out?

explain.say: Last, the trend tops out: almost everyone who will join has joined, and the line flattens. Then a new craze begins! Joining in can be fun, just ask yourself: would I still want this if nobody else did? Great work! Wow fact: the word comes from the bandwagon, a cart carrying a band in American parades in the 1800s.

faq.a: The bandwagon effect is our tendency to do or believe something mainly because many other people do. The more people join, the more others want to join.
asks: What does jumping on the bandwagon mean?

faq.a: A few people, often early adopters or famous people, try something new. If others notice and like it, it starts to spread.
asks: Tell me about a few start

faq.q: Why do trends suddenly spread so fast?
faq.a: Each new person who joins makes the thing look more popular, which persuades even more people to join. This feedback makes the line shoot up.

faq.q: What is fear of missing out?
faq.a: Fear of missing out, or FOMO, is the worried feeling that others are enjoying something without you. It pushes people to join trends so they are not left out.
asks: Tell me about fear of missing out

faq.a: When almost everyone who will join has joined, there is nobody new to join, and the novelty wears off. People then look for the next new thing.
asks: Tell me about trend tops out

facts: The phrase "jump on the bandwagon" grew from US politics in the 1800s, when candidates rode circus bandwagons in parades and supporters climbed aboard.
S-shaped curves like this one also describe how new technologies spread, an idea studied by Everett Rogers in "Diffusion of Innovations" (1962).
